newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden dismisses anti-EMU report as rumour.
newsitem.headline: Sweden dismisses anti-EMU report as rumour.

text.p: Sweden's Prime Minister Goran Persson dismissed rumours on Wednesday that he was more negative in private than in public towards Swedish membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Swedish bond yields opened higher on Wednesday morning in part on an article in Swedish daily Svenska Dagbladet quoting anonymous sources saying that the Swedish government was opposed to Swedish membership of EMU.

The newspaper quoted a source as saying Persson, along with Finance Minister Erik Asbrink, would not openly admit that they were against Swedish EMU membership as they feared interest rates would rise.

But Persson dismissed the report as speculation and said the ruling Social Democratic party would reveal its view on EMU before the end of May. Debt yields recovered during the day, but took their cue from foreign markets and a stronger crown.
"Rumours, rumours, rumours," Persson told Reuters. "There are too many rumours and too few facts on this discussion."
"Before the end of this month, the Social Democratic party will announce its stance," Persson said. "That is what we have said for a long time and we will stick to that."
He declined to give a more exact date.
Other government members have been vague lately, talking about an announcement in a few weeks' time.
A party congress is then expected to vote about a possible link in September and a parliamentary ruling will follow before the end of the year.

Although a decision to keep Sweden outside EMU in 1999 has to a large extent been factored in by market players, economists expect interest rates to edge higher and the crown to soften somewhat when the official statement is released.
Some analysts say the main obstacle to Swedish EMU memebership is low popular support.

Although opinion polls have shown people turning slightly more in favour of EMU, a survey earlier this month showed only 26 percent supported 1999 membership, while 24 percent wanted to join at a later stage and 35 percent were against a link.
The rest were undecided.
"Many within the Social Democratic party are against monetary union. Not the leaders, but the people," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Stephanie Pfeiffer.
"For that reason I believe there will be a 'soft no,' that they will say Sweden should not join in 1999 but should keep the door open to join later," she said.
Sven-Arne Svensson, an economist at Stockholm brokerage Hagstromer & Qviberg, said a 'soft yes' to EMU was more likely than a 'soft no.'
"I believe the government will choose as weak a formulation as possible. I think they would like to have an opening for Sweden to join in 1999 if public opinion turns," Svensson said.
Svenska Dagbladet quoted the unnamed source as saying Persson was "worried that Sweden will be a vassal state, that EMU will force us into such a situation."
Another source, which the newspaper said was from the party top, said the government's position, when it was unveiled, would not be clear cut.
"The wording will be woolly," the source was quoted as saying.
